title: Chillán to Lima: The Road of the Liberator of Chile
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: El Huacho de Chillán: The Natural Son

stops.name: Chillán Viejo, the birth house under the volcano
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint Bernard a boy is born in Chillán, in sight of the smoking volcano, to Isabel Riquelme, eighteen years old. His father is Ambrosio O'Higgins, the Irishman rising through the King's service, soon Governor of Chile, then Viceroy of Peru, who will pay for the boy from a distance all his life and never once let the child look upon his face. The tradition marks it as the founding wound of the nation: the Padre de la Patria begins as the huacho, the unacknowledged son, carrying his mother's name Riquelme.
suggested_refs: Parque Monumental Bernardo O'Higgins in Chillán Viejo, with the 60-metre mural of his life carved in stone

stops.name: Talca, the house of Juan Albano Pereira
stops.campa: The infant is carried north to Talca and given into the house of don Juan Albano Pereira, merchant of the town and partner of the distant father. Here the boy learns his first letters and calls Albano's wife mamita. The canon dwells on the house itself, for fate has marked its walls: thirty-six years later, in this same room where the huacho played on the floor, the grown man will sign the Act of Independence of Chile. The tradition says the house waited for him.
suggested_refs: Casa Albano, today the Museo O'Higginiano y de Bellas Artes de Talca, the room of childhood and of the signing
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, Vida del capitán general don Bernardo O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Chillán, the Colegio de Naturales of the Franciscans
stops.campa: The boy returns to his mother's town and enters the Franciscan Colegio de Naturales, the school kept for the sons of Mapuche caciques. He sits on the same benches as the boys of Araucanía, learns their games and their tongue, and the friars teach them all one catechism. The canon reads the seed here: the Liberator who will one day abolish titles of nobility and dream a single citizenry learned as a child that the huacho and the cacique's son share one bench and one bread.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan convent records of Chillán; the Mapudungun phrases O'Higgins still used in his last years at Montalván

stops.name: Lima, the Convictorio de San Carlos
stops.campa: At the father's silent command the boy is shipped north to Lima and placed under the merchant Juan Ignacio Blake, to study at the Colegio de San Carlos. Ambrosio is now the greatest man in Chile and soon in all Peru; the son lives streets away from the father's palace and is never received. The canon savors the cruelty of the arrangement: the Viceroy watches the boy's accounts through agents, corrects his schooling by letter, and keeps his face turned away. In Lima the boy first hears the murmurs against Spain.
suggested_refs: The Casona de San Marcos (former Convictorio) on the Parque Universitario, Lima
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, Vida del capitán general don Bernardo O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Callao, embarkation for Spain
stops.campa: Sixteen years old, the boy Bernardo Riquelme is put aboard ship at Callao, bound around the Horn for Cádiz and thence to England, to be finished as a gentleman of commerce. The father has decreed it from behind his curtain. The boy leaves the Pacific of his birth not knowing he will not smell it again for eight years, nor that he sails toward the man who will hand him his destiny. The tradition counts this the first of the three great sea-crossings that frame his life.
suggested_refs: The Callao waterfront and fortress of Real Felipe, which he will see again as an exile in 1823

segments.name: El Discípulo de Miranda: The Atlantic and the Oath

stops.name: Cádiz, the house of Nicolás de la Cruz
stops.campa: The ship raises the white towers of Cádiz. The boy lodges with don Nicolás de la Cruz y Bahamonde, merchant of Talca grown rich in the Indies trade, his father's correspondent and now his keeper. Cádiz is the funnel of empire: silver in, decrees out. The boy watches the machinery of the monopoly that strangles his Chile. De la Cruz forwards him on to London with letters, an allowance, and instructions to learn English commerce. The allowance will prove a chain.
suggested_refs: The merchant houses of the Calle Nueva, Cádiz; Nicolás de la Cruz's later title, Conde de Maule

stops.name: Richmond upon Thames, the English schooling
stops.campa: The young man is placed at a Catholic academy in Richmond, on the green bend of the Thames, while the watchmakers Spencer and Perkins of London hold his purse, and skim it, so that the son of the Viceroy of Peru goes hungry and patches his own coat. He studies history, geography, French, drawing and music; he paints a miniature of himself and ships it to his mother in Chillán, the only face of him she will have for twenty years. In Richmond the orphan of empire becomes a man of the Enlightenment.
suggested_refs: The miniature portrait of young Bernardo painted in England and sent to Isabel Riquelme
The blue plaque tradition of O'Higgins in Richmond, Clarence House

stops.name: London, Grafton Way, the school of Francisco de Miranda
stops.campa: In the house of Francisco de Miranda the true education begins. The Venezuelan, veteran of three revolutions, the Precursor, takes the lonely Chilean as his pupil, ostensibly in mathematics. But between the theorems Miranda unrolls the map of a continent and names the disease: Spain. Night after night at Grafton Way the master pours into the young man the whole doctrine of American emancipation. O'Higgins will say afterward that whatever he became was kindled in these rooms. The canon calls him first of the disciples, first-fruits of the Precursor's sowing.
suggested_refs: Miranda's house at 58 Grafton Way, London, still standing with its plaque
Miranda's London archive, the Colombeia
sources: Ricardo Donoso, El pensamiento vivo de O'Higgins

stops.name: London, the oath of the Rational Knights
stops.campa: In a shuttered room by candlelight, before Miranda as Grand Master of the Gran Reunión Americana, Bernardo kneels with his hand on a sword and is initiated into the lodge of the Caballeros Racionales. He swears never to recognize any government of his homeland not chosen by the free will of its peoples, and to work unto death for the independence of America. The oath is administered, witnessed, and sealed in secrecy. From this night the huacho of Chillán is a sworn soldier of a country that does not yet exist.
stops.quote: Nunca reconoceré por gobierno legítimo de mi patria sino a aquel que sea elegido por la libre y espontánea voluntad de los pueblos, y trabajaré por la independencia de América.
stops.quote_source: Oath formula of the Lautarine lodges, preserved in the lodge tradition (Eyzaguirre, La Logia Lautarina; Lautaro Lodge constitutions)
suggested_refs: The constitutions of the Logia Lautaro, whose Chilean redaction O'Higgins himself later drafted

stops.name: London, Miranda's counsels of farewell
stops.campa: The pupil must go home. Miranda writes out for him the Consejos de un viejo sudamericano a un joven compatriota: trust no man over forty save a very few; beware the Inquisition's spies in every port; guard the secret as your life. He orders Bernardo to memorize the letter and burn it. Bernardo memorizes it and does not burn it: he sews it into the lining of his hat, and under that hat the revolution crosses the Atlantic. The canon counts the letter among the founding scriptures of the patria.
suggested_refs: Miranda's letter 'Consejos de un viejo sudamericano', 1799, the text preserved and printed (Memoria Chilena)

stops.name: Cádiz, detained at the gate of the war
stops.campa: He reaches Cádiz to find the ocean closed: England's fleets blockade the bay and no ship sails for the Indies. He waits in the house of de la Cruz, and the waiting turns poisonous: word of his London friendships has run ahead of him through Spain's spies, and the name Miranda beside the name Riquelme is denounced to the very ministers his father serves. The old Viceroy in Lima, informed that his unacknowledged son consorts with the arch-traitor, strikes him from his will in wrath. The disciple pays his first price.
suggested_refs: The denunciations of the Spanish agents in London reporting Miranda's visitors
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, Vida del capitán general don Bernardo O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: The bay of Cádiz, the capture of the Confianza
stops.campa: On 3 April 1800 he embarks at last on the frigate Confianza for the Indies. Barely at sea, an English cruiser runs her down and takes her; Bernardo loses baggage and money and is set back on the shore he sailed from, stripped to his shirt. The canon reads the omen plainly: the sea will not carry him home until he has been scoured of everything (inheritance, name, patron and purse) and made ready to receive the patria as his only property.
suggested_refs: Shipping registers of Cádiz for the frigate Confianza, April 1800

stops.name: Cádiz, the yellow fever and the father's legacy
stops.campa: The great yellow-fever epidemic of 1800 falls on Cádiz, and Bernardo falls with it. Ten thousand die around him; he lies at the door of death and is spared. As he rises, news crosses the ocean: Ambrosio O'Higgins, Viceroy of Peru, died in Lima on 18 March 1801, and at the very end, the father relented. A codicil recognizes the son and leaves him the hacienda of Las Canteras with its thousands of cattle. The father acknowledges the son only from the far side of the grave; they never exchanged a living word.
suggested_refs: Ambrosio O'Higgins's testament and codicil, Lima 1801

stops.name: Valparaíso, the homecoming
stops.campa: On 6 September 1802 the hills of Valparaíso rise out of the sea and Bernardo steps ashore in Chile after eight years, carrying Miranda's letter in the lining of his hat and his dead father's name newly his own. No one meets him; he is a stranger in his patria. The canon pauses on the image: the future Supreme Director standing unknown on the same shore from which he will one day launch the squadrons that free the Pacific.
suggested_refs: The port registers of Valparaíso, September 1802

stops.name: Chillán, the mother's embrace
stops.campa: He rides south to Chillán and after twelve years stands before doña Isabel Riquelme and his half-sister Rosa. The mother receives the son she surrendered as an infant; from this hour the three are never truly parted again: Isabel and Rosa will follow him over the cordillera into exile and to the end in Lima. Here he takes up publicly the name O'Higgins, the dead Viceroy's gift, and the canon notes the transformation: Bernardo Riquelme, the hidden child, has become don Bernardo O'Higgins, vecino of the south.
suggested_refs: Portrait tradition of doña Isabel Riquelme, Museo Histórico Nacional

stops.name: Hacienda Las Canteras, taking possession
stops.campa: He takes possession of Las Canteras on the Isla de la Laja: leagues of pasture under the Antuco volcano, four thousand head of cattle, the frontier of Araucanía at the fence line. The disciple of Miranda becomes a farmer, and a good one: he plants vines, breeds horses, trades with the Pehuenche across the Biobío in their own tongue. The canon keeps this decade as the hidden years, the Liberator ploughing like Cincinnatus while the letter in the hat lining waits for its hour.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Las Canteras, burned by royalists in 1813, the sacrificed patrimony

stops.name: Los Ángeles, alcalde and man of the frontier
stops.campa: The vecinos of the Laja make him alcalde of the cabildo of Los Ángeles and subdelegate of the frontier partido. He drains marshes, lays out roads, holds parleys with the caciques, and quietly measures the men around him against the coming test. Spain, meanwhile, decays audibly: the news of Trafalgar, then of the King's captivity at Bayonne, arrives over the cordillera like distant thunder. The canon shows him reading the gazettes at Las Canteras and writing to trusted friends that the hour Miranda foretold is drawing near.
suggested_refs: Cabildo acts of Los Ángeles, 1806-1810
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, Vida del capitán general don Bernardo O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Las Canteras, the news of the Junta of Santiago
stops.campa: A rider brings word from the capital: on 18 September a Junta of Government has been sworn in Santiago in the name of the captive King. O'Higgins reads through the loyal formulas to the fire underneath: Miranda's fire. He arms his inquilinos, forms two militia companies of his own horsemen at his own cost, and drills them on the pastures of Las Canteras. The canon marks it precisely: while others debate, the man of the Laja is already raising the first soldiers of what will become the Army of Chile.
suggested_refs: The militia rolls of the Isla de la Laja, 1810-1811

stops.name: Santiago, deputy in the first National Congress
stops.campa: On 4 July 1811 the first National Congress of Chile opens in Santiago and O'Higgins takes his seat as deputy for Los Ángeles. He sits with the exaltados, the party of full independence, and works the corridors with a paper hidden in his coat: the plan of secret organization he has drawn from Miranda's constitutions. It is O'Higgins, the canon holds, who gives the brotherhood its Chilean name: Lautaro, after the Mapuche boy who learned the conqueror's art and turned it against him. The huacho schooled among caciques names the revolution for one.
suggested_refs: The rolls of the Primer Congreso Nacional, 1811

stops.name: El Roble on the Itata, the charge that made the general
stops.campa: At dawn on 17 October 1813 the royalists surprise the patriot camp at the Roble ford of the Itata. The line breaks; men drown in the river; the day is lost. Then O'Higgins arrives at the gallop, seizes the musket of a soldier shot dead beside him, and though a ball tears through his leg he stands in the ford and cries the words the nation will carve on his monuments. The routed army turns behind him and throws the royalists back across the river. From this wound and this cry, the canon dates his generalship.
stops.quote: ¡O vivir con honor, o morir con gloria! ¡El que sea valiente, que me siga!
stops.quote_source: Battle tradition of El Roble, 17 October 1813, as preserved by the Chilean Army and the chroniclers (Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile)
suggested_refs: The monolith at Paso El Roble near Quillón
The phrase inscribed on the O'Higgins equestrian monument, Santiago

stops.name: Concepción, General in Chief of the Army
stops.campa: The Junta strips José Miguel Carrera of the command and gives it to the wounded colonel of El Roble. At Concepción O'Higgins takes up an army that is hungry, unpaid and half-shod, in a province the royalists are devouring from the sea. The Carreras never forgive him the promotion, and the canon opens here the fratricidal wound of the Patria Vieja: two houses, Carrera and O'Higgins, quarreling over the cradle of the republic while Abascal's regiments land from Peru.
suggested_refs: The Junta's decree of command, late 1813
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: El Quilo and Membrillar, the two days on the Itata
stops.campa: On 19 and 20 March 1814 the war doubles its drumbeat: O'Higgins forces the crossing at El Quilo, and a day later stands with Mackenna in the entrenchments of Membrillar as Gaínza's whole army breaks against them. Powder smoke lies on the Itata for two days; the patriot squares hold. The canon pairs the battles like twin hinges: the moment the improvised militias of Chile prove they can stand in open field against the veterans of the King.
suggested_refs: Juan Mackenna's dispatches from Membrillar, March 1814
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: Quechereguas, the road to Santiago barred
stops.campa: Gaínza slips north for Santiago; O'Higgins, outmarching him by forced night marches with an army on bleeding feet, throws himself across the road at the casas of Quechereguas on the Claro. On 8 April the royalists assault the position three times and three times are hurled back. The capital never sees the enemy. The canon loves the arithmetic of the feat, the slower army arriving first, and reads in it the O'Higgins signature: not elegance, but an immovable body placed between Chile and its destruction.
suggested_refs: The casas de Quechereguas on the Río Claro
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: The banks of the Lircay, the treaty signed under protest
stops.campa: On 3 May 1814, under the guns of the English commodore Hillyar's mediation, O'Higgins signs the Treaty of Lircay: Chile to acknowledge the King, the royalists to leave; hostages exchanged; the flags of the Patria Vieja furled. He signs as a soldier who cannot feed his men, and the canon absolves him with the sequel: the Viceroy in Lima repudiates the treaty within weeks and sends Osorio with fresh regiments. The parchment of Lircay becomes the proof text that with Spain there is no peace but submission: independence or nothing.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Lircay text, May 1814
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: Las Tres Acequias, patriot blood by patriot hands
stops.campa: The quarrel of the two houses comes to powder: Carrera has retaken the government by coup, and on 26 August 1814, at the three irrigation channels south of the Maipo, O'Higgins's division and Carrera's fire on one another. Patriot kills patriot within earshot of the advancing enemy. The canon narrates the day as the national sin of the Patria Vieja; its expiation follows at once, for word arrives that Osorio is over the Cachapoal, and O'Higgins, swallowing the feud whole, puts himself and his men under Carrera's orders to face the invader.
suggested_refs: The plain of Las Tres Acequias near San Bernardo
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: Rancagua, the first day of the siege
stops.campa: On the morning of 1 October 1814 Osorio's five thousand close the four streets of Rancagua upon O'Higgins and seventeen hundred men behind trenches of adobe and carts. Summoned to surrender, O'Higgins answers by hoisting a black flag over the tower of the plaza church: no quarter asked, none given. All day the assaults break against the trenches; the defenders' water is cut; the wounded are dragged into the church. On the hill to the north, Carrera's third division stands watching, and the promised relief does not come.
suggested_refs: The black flag of Rancagua in the national tradition
The tower of the Iglesia de la Merced, Rancagua, still bearing bullet scars

stops.name: Rancagua, the breakout through the flames
stops.campa: Thirty-three hours into the siege the town burns around the survivors, the cannon are out of grape, and the last water is gone. O'Higgins, twice wounded, mounts what horses remain and gives the order the nation still recites. Two hundred horsemen burst from the plaza through fire and bayonets, O'Higgins at the point, and cut their way clean through Osorio's army into the open valley. The Patria Vieja dies at Rancagua, but its seed escapes on horseback through the flames. The canon calls the breakout the baptism of fire of the Chilean nation.
stops.quote: ¡Los Dragones a caballo! ¡Monte a caballo todo el que pueda! ¡Nos abriremos paso en medio del enemigo!
stops.quote_source: Battle tradition of Rancagua, 2 October 1814 (Academia de Historia Militar de Chile; Barros Arana)
suggested_refs: Juan Manuel Blanes's painting 'La batalla de Rancagua' (1872)
The plaza of Rancagua with its monument to the defenders

stops.name: The Uspallata pass, the emigration over the Andes
stops.campa: The remnant of a nation goes up into the cordillera: soldiers with bound wounds, friars, women with children on mules, among them doña Isabel and Rosa, the Liberator's mother and sister, riding with the baggage of defeat. O'Higgins, his wounds still open, shepherds the column through the October snows of the Uspallata route. Behind them Las Canteras is ash and the royalist terror begins; ahead is Mendoza and an unknown governor named San Martín. The canon frames the crossing as the nation's exodus: Chile carried over the mountains in saddlebags.
suggested_refs: The Uspallata valley and the old cordillera trail of the emigrados
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: Mendoza, the meeting with San Martín
stops.campa: The Governor-Intendant of Cuyo rides out to receive the defeated. José de San Martín and Bernardo O'Higgins clasp hands for the first time: two initiates of the same London lodge, meeting as if by countersign. San Martín, weighing the exiles, sides with O'Higgins against Carrera's pretensions, and around these two the great design takes shape: an army forged in Mendoza to retake Chile and carry the war by sea to Lima itself. The canon dates the continental strategy of liberation from this handclasp.
suggested_refs: The Área Fundacional of old Mendoza, where the emigrados were received

stops.name: El Plumerillo, forging the Army of the Andes
stops.campa: On the dusty camp ground of El Plumerillo north of Mendoza the Army of the Andes is hammered into being, and O'Higgins drills the Chilean units day after day: the escapees of Rancagua now sergeants, the huachos and inquilinos now grenadiers. Fray Luis Beltrán casts cannon in his forge like a warrior-monk; the women of Cuyo sew uniforms; San Martín spreads false maps for the Viceroy's spies. O'Higgins is given command of a division. Two years of exile are compressed into one instrument of war.
suggested_refs: The Campo Histórico El Plumerillo, Mendoza

stops.name: Mendoza, the blessing of the flag and the Virgin made General
stops.campa: On 5 January 1817, before the army drawn up in the plaza of Mendoza, the new flag of the Andes is blessed and Our Lady of Carmen is proclaimed Patroness and Generala of the army; San Martín lays his baton in her hand. O'Higgins stands at the head of his division as the standard dips before the image. The campaign that follows is fought, the canon insists, under her mantle: every dispatch of victory will be laid at her feet, and O'Higgins will yet build her a temple on a battlefield not yet chosen.
suggested_refs: The flag of the Army of the Andes, preserved in Mendoza's Casa de Gobierno
The image of the Virgen del Carmen de Cuyo

stops.name: The Paso de los Patos, commanding a column across the roof of America
stops.campa: The army goes up by six passes at once, and O'Higgins leads a division of the main body over the Paso de los Patos: four thousand metres of wind and scree, mules dying by the hundred, cannon dismounted and dragged on sledges of hide. He rides the column front to rear in the thin air, the man of the hot Laja valleys now a commander in the ice. On the far side lies Chile. The canon sets the crossing beside Hannibal's and gives O'Higgins his place in it: not a passenger of the epic, but a driver of it.
suggested_refs: The route of Los Patos through the Valle Hermoso, San Juan

stops.name: Las Coimas, valley of Putaendo, first blood in Chile
stops.campa: The vanguard comes down out of the rocks into the green of Putaendo, and at Las Coimas on 7 February the patriot horse scatters the royalist advance parties. The army of the exiles stands again on Chilean soil, two years and four months after the flames of Rancagua. Guasos come down from the hills with fruit and intelligence; the valley declares itself. O'Higgins presses the columns toward the cuesta of Chacabuco, where Marcó del Pont's army gathers to bar the road to Santiago.
suggested_refs: The battlefield marker at Las Coimas, Putaendo

stops.name: Chacabuco, the charge of 12 February 1817
stops.campa: The plan gives O'Higgins the eastern road and orders him to wait for Soler's flanking column. Before noon, seeing the royalists forming to escape the trap, O'Higgins waits no longer: he hurls his fifteen hundred straight at the line with the bayonet. The first charge is thrown back from the ravines; he re-forms and charges again as Soler's guns open on the flank, and the royalist army disintegrates. By dusk the road to Santiago is open and the Reconquista is dead. San Martín's plan won the campaign, says the canon, but the arrebato of O'Higgins won the day.
suggested_refs: Pedro Subercaseaux's painting 'La batalla de Chacabuco'
The Cristo and battle monument on the cuesta de Chacabuco

stops.name: Santiago, Supreme Director of Chile
stops.campa: Santiago pours into the streets to receive the victors. An open cabildo offers the supreme command to San Martín, who refuses it: his road runs to Lima. On 16 February 1817 the assembly acclaims Bernardo O'Higgins Supreme Director of Chile. The huacho of Chillán, denied his father's face, now bears the fatherhood of the nation itself. He takes the office as the lodge intended: not a throne but a lever, to finish the war in the south and build the fleet that will carry the revolution to Peru.
suggested_refs: José Gil de Castro's portrait of O'Higgins as Supreme Director (1820)

stops.name: Talcahuano, the assault on the last fortress
stops.campa: The war is not finished: the royalist remnant fortifies the peninsula of Talcahuano, and through the southern winter O'Higgins directs the siege in person, back on the ground of his first campaigns. On 6 December 1817 he launches the great night assault against the trenches; the columns carry the first works and break against the second, and the ditches fill with the bravest of the army. He raises the siege when word comes that Osorio has landed again from Peru with a new invasion. The canon keeps Talcahuano as the hard lesson before the crown of Maipú.
suggested_refs: The heights of Talcahuano and the old Spanish battery lines
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: Concepción, the proclamation of independence
stops.campa: On the first day of 1818, in the plaza of Concepción with Osorio's invasion fleet already at sea, O'Higgins proclaims what the cautious have postponed for eight years: Chile is, and of right ought to be, free. The Act is dated this day from Concepción: the declaration made not from a safe capital but from the war's front porch, an answer flung at the approaching enemy. The canon relishes the defiance of the timing: independence declared precisely when Spain comes strongest to prevent it.
stops.quote: La fuerza ha sido la razón suprema que por más de trescientos años ha mantenido al Nuevo Mundo en la necesidad de venerar como un dogma la usurpación de sus derechos.
stops.quote_source: Acta de la Independencia de Chile, dated Concepción, 1 January 1818, issued and signed by O'Higgins as Supreme Director
suggested_refs: The Acta de la Independencia (original perished in the fire of the Palacio de La Moneda, 1973, the relic's own martyrdom)

stops.name: Talca, the oath sworn in the house of his childhood
stops.campa: On 12 February 1818, first anniversary of Chacabuco, O'Higgins signs and swears the Declaration of Independence at Talca, in the very house of Juan Albano where he lived as a nameless child; the same day, before the delegate director in Santiago's plaza, the whole people raise their right hands. The circle the canon drew at his cradle closes: the room that sheltered the huacho witnesses the birth certificate of the nation. Bells, salvos and Te Deums run the length of the valley while Osorio's army marches north against the newborn state.
stops.quote: Juro a Dios y prometo a la patria, bajo la garantía de mi honor, vida y fortuna, sostener la presente declaración de independencia.
stops.quote_source: Oath formula of the Jura de la Independencia, 12 February 1818
suggested_refs: Pedro Subercaseaux's painting 'La Jura de la Independencia de Chile'
The signing room in the Museo O'Higginiano de Talca

stops.name: Cancha Rayada, the night of the shattered arm
stops.campa: On the night of 19 March 1818, at Cancha Rayada outside Talca, Osorio's veterans fall on the patriot camp in the dark. The army is thrown into chaos; guns are lost; a musket ball shatters O'Higgins's right arm as he tries to stem the rout. Word runs to Santiago that the army is destroyed, that San Martín is dead, that O'Higgins is dead. But Las Heras brings three thousand men off unbroken, and the wounded Director, refusing amputation, rides north with his arm in a sling to show himself alive. The nation holds its breath.
suggested_refs: The monument of Cancha Rayada in Talca

stops.name: Santiago, 'Aún tenemos patria, ciudadanos'
stops.campa: Panic empties Santiago's strongboxes toward Mendoza until Manuel Rodríguez, the guerrillero of the lodge, wheels his horse in the plaza and cries that there is still a fatherland, citizens, and raises a regiment of clerks and artisans, the Húsares de la Muerte, in an afternoon. Into this fevered city rides O'Higgins, gray with pain, his arm bound, and the sight of the living Director turns terror into fury. He pours every man and peso toward the plain of Maipo where San Martín reassembles the army for the final throw.
suggested_refs: The black uniform and skull standard of the Húsares de la Muerte
sources: Diego Barros Arana, Historia General de Chile

stops.name: The plain of Maipú, the battle and the abrazo
stops.campa: On 5 April 1818 San Martín breaks Osorio's army on the plain of Maipú in the decisive battle of the south. O'Higgins, forbidden by his wound to command, cannot stay away: at the crisis of the afternoon he arrives from Santiago at the head of a thousand militia, his arm in a sling, and rides through the smoke to San Martín. He throws his good arm around the victor's neck with the words the two nations have repeated ever since; San Martín answers that Chile will never forget the illustrious invalid who came to the field in such a state. The embrace of Maipú seals the freedom of Chile.
stops.quote_source: The Abrazo de Maipú, 5 April 1818, as recorded in the battle tradition (Instituto Nacional Sanmartiniano; Barros Arana)
suggested_refs: Pedro Subercaseaux's painting 'El abrazo de Maipú'
The Templo Votivo de Maipú, built on the field in fulfilment of the vow to the Virgen del Carmen

stops.name: Valparaíso, the First National Squadron sails
stops.campa: O'Higgins has begged, taxed and mortgaged a navy into existence: four ships bought and armed at a bankrupt nation's cost. On 10 October 1818 the First National Squadron under Blanco Encalada stands out of Valparaíso to hunt the Spanish convoy, and the Director watches from the height above the port. Turning to those beside him he speaks the sentence the Armada keeps as its founding prophecy, measuring Columbus's three caravels against his own four hulls. Within the month the squadron takes the frigate María Isabel and the sea begins to change owners.
stops.quote: Tres barquichuelos dieron a los reyes de España la posesión del Nuevo Mundo; estas cuatro tablas van a quitársela.
stops.quote_source: Tradition of the Armada de Chile, departure of the First National Squadron, 10 October 1818
suggested_refs: The captured Spanish frigate María Isabel, renamed O'Higgins
The heights of Cerro Alegre, Valparaíso

stops.name: Valparaíso, Cochrane comes to the flag
stops.campa: On 28 November 1818 Lord Thomas Cochrane, the sea-wolf of the Aix Roads, steps ashore at Valparaíso to take command of the squadron O'Higgins has built for him. The Director gives the Radical Lord his fleet and his mission: sweep the Pacific, break Callao, prepare the water road to Lima. Between the huaso Director and the Scottish firebrand there will be storms of pride and pay. The canon does not hide them. But under their joined hands Chile becomes, for one blazing decade, the naval power of the Pacific.
suggested_refs: Cochrane's flagship O'Higgins (ex-María Isabel)
The Museo Marítimo Nacional, Valparaíso

stops.name: Valparaíso, the Liberating Expedition of Peru sails
stops.campa: On 20 August 1820, his forty-second birthday, O'Higgins stands above Valparaíso as the Liberating Expedition of Peru puts to sea: Cochrane's warships shepherding sixteen transports, San Martín and four thousand soldiers bound for the coast of the Viceroyalty. It is the largest armament the new world's south has ever launched, paid for by Chile's last peso, the fulfilment of the design drawn in Mendoza and, further back, in Miranda's rooms at Grafton Way. The Director watches the sails diminish toward the destiny of a continent, and the canon fixes him there: the giver of the fleet, remaining behind.
suggested_refs: The embarkation rolls of the Expedición Libertadora del Perú

segments.name: El Director Supremo y la Abdicación

stops.name: Santiago, the builder's years and the gathering shadows
stops.campa: The Director builds as he fought, frontally: the Alameda de las Delicias laid out over the old river branch, the Escuela Militar, the Cementerio General consecrated in 1821, the markets, the night watch, the abolition of titles of nobility and of bullfights, ships and schools. But the ledger of the lodge has dark entries the canon does not conceal: Manuel Rodríguez shot at Til Til, the Carrera brothers dead before Mendoza firing squads, and the aristocracy he has humbled whispering in every parlor. The hero of Rancagua governs a peace more treacherous than any siege.
suggested_refs: The Cementerio General of Santiago, his own foundation, where his mausoleum would one day stand
The Alameda de las Delicias

stops.name: Santiago, the Constitution of 1822 and the storm
stops.campa: In October 1822 a convention promulgates a new Constitution that could prolong the Director's rule for years, and the country's patience breaks. Concepción rises behind General Freire; the provinces disown the capital; the treasury is empty from paying for Peru's liberation, and an earthquake has flattened Valparaíso as if the ground itself voted. O'Higgins, the man who charged at Chacabuco without orders, now faces the one enemy that cannot be charged: the turning of his own people. The canon sets the scene for the noblest act of his life.
suggested_refs: The text of the Constitution of 1822

stops.name: Santiago, sala del Consulado, the abdication and the bared chest
stops.campa: On 28 January 1823, before an open cabildo of two hundred notables in the hall of the Consulado, O'Higgins lays down the supreme power rather than light a civil war. He swears in the junta that replaces him, then turns to the assembly that has muttered accusations for months, tears open his uniform coat, and offers them his bare chest: if his faults must be purged in blood, let them take their vengeance now. The hall that came to depose him erupts instead in vivas. He walks out a private citizen, greater in the fall, says the canon, than in all his victories.
stops.quote: Estoy dispuesto a contestar todas las acusaciones que se me hagan; y si esas faltas han causado desgracias que no pueden purgarse más que con mi sangre, tomad de mí la venganza que queráis. Aquí está mi pecho.
stops.quote_source: Abdication speech, cabildo abierto of Santiago, 28 January 1823 (Barros Arana; Academia de Historia Militar de Chile)
suggested_refs: The painting 'La abdicación de O'Higgins' (Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes / SURDOC)

stops.name: Valparaíso, embarking on the brig Fly
stops.campa: Held half a year under courteous guard while his enemies audit his rule and find nothing to seize, O'Higgins is at last permitted to go. On 17 July 1823 he boards the English brig Fly at Valparaíso with his mother, his sister Rosa and his small son Demetrio, bound for Peru, he says for a season, for his health. The hills of the port drop below the horizon. He is forty-four years old, and he will never see Chile again. The canon marks the third sea-crossing, the one with no return.
suggested_refs: The sailing of the Fly in the port records of Valparaíso, July 1823
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, El ostracismo de O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Callao and Lima, the exile received with honors
stops.campa: The Fly raises the island of San Lorenzo and the fortress of the Real Felipe, and O'Higgins lands at Callao: the port of his boyhood voyages, now half-free, half-Spanish, wholly at war. Lima receives the Liberator of Chile with salutes and a house; the government he helped to free by sea votes him honors. He walks streets he walked as the Viceroy's hidden son; the palace his father ruled from stands a musket shot from his lodgings. The canon savors the return of the huacho to the father's city, this time with a liberator's name.
suggested_refs: The fortress of Real Felipe, Callao
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, El ostracismo de O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Lima, the meeting with Bolívar
stops.campa: Simón Bolívar enters Lima on the first of September 1823 to take up the last campaign of the continental war, and the two liberators meet. At the banquet the Venezuelan raises his glass to the hero of Chacabuco; O'Higgins, who has commanded nations, answers that he comes to serve the freedom of America in whatever rank is given him, as a simple soldier if need be. Miranda's two greatest disciples, the canon observes, close the circle of the Precursor: the one finishing the war the other's fleets made possible.
suggested_refs: The banquet toasts of September 1823 as recorded in the Lima gazettes
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, El ostracismo de O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: The sierra road, too late for Ayacucho
stops.campa: When Bolívar's army marches into the sierra in 1824, O'Higgins rides after it to serve in the last battle of the American war. He climbs the freezing punas by Jauja toward the theatre of decision, and on the mountain road the couriers meet him with the news: on 9 December, at Ayacucho, Sucre has destroyed the Viceroy's army; the war of three hundred years is over. The canon gives him the exile's peculiar grief: he weeps that America is free and that her last battle was fought without him, turns his horse, and rides back down to the coast a farmer.
suggested_refs: The pampa of Ayacucho and the capitulation of 9 December 1824
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, El ostracismo de O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Hacienda Montalván, Cañete, the planter of the exile
stops.campa: Peru's gratitude gives him the haciendas of Montalván and Cuiba in the warm valley of Cañete, and there the Liberator becomes again what he was on the Laja: a farmer. He plants cane and cotton, doctors his laborers, keeps Chilean wine for Chilean visitors, and writes letter after letter home, to friends, to governments that do not answer, offering his sword in every war Chile fights, urging always one obsession: that Chile must seize and settle the Strait of Magellan before another flag does. Under the fig trees of Montalván, doña Isabel grows old; the canon calls these the years of the long patience.
suggested_refs: The Casa Hacienda Montalván, San Vicente de Cañete, still standing
The Magellan letters of the O'Higgins epistolario
sources: Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, El ostracismo de O'Higgins (1860)

stops.name: Lima, the death of doña Isabel Riquelme
stops.campa: On 21 April 1839 doña Isabel Riquelme dies in exile, the mother who bore the huacho at eighteen, followed him over the burning cordillera at fifty-six, and kept his house through every banishment. O'Higgins buries her in Lima's earth, far from Chillán, and something of his own root is cut. Rosa remains, the sister-companion of the whole long road. The canon keeps doña Isabel as the silent co-founder of the patria: the woman whose constancy carried the Liberator before the Liberator carried the nation.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Isabel Riquelme, later repatriated to Chile

stops.name: Montalván and Lima, the restitution and the packed trunks
stops.campa: In 1842 Chile at last turns its face back to him: the government of Bulnes restores the Captain General to the army's rolls with his rank and pay, and letters arrive inviting the Padre de la Patria home. The old man's joy is boyish; he settles his accounts, packs his trunks, and moves down to Lima to take ship for Valparaíso. But his heart, worn out by the long roads, falters as the voyage nears. The doctors forbid the sea. He waits in Lima through the winter, Chile visible, so to speak, from his window, while his strength runs out.
suggested_refs: The restitution decree of 1842 in the Chilean army rolls

stops.name: Lima, calle Espaderos, 'Magallanes! Magallanes!'
stops.campa: At half past noon on 24 October 1842, in his house on the calle Espaderos, the heart of Bernardo O'Higgins stops. Around the bed stand Rosa, his son Pedro Demetrio, and the Mapuche women who followed him from the Laja twenty years before. In the last labor of his breathing his mind flies not backward to his battles but southward and forward, to the strait at the bottom of the world he has begged Chile to claim, and he cries out the name: Magallanes! Magallanes! Eight months later a Chilean schooner plants the flag on the Strait, obedient to the dying word. The exile's last breath founds a territory.
stops.quote_source: Deathbed tradition, Lima, 24 October 1842, as recorded by those present and preserved by the Chilean Armada and the chroniclers
suggested_refs: The goleta Ancud's expedition to the Strait of Magellan, 1843
His first tomb in Lima's Cementerio Presbítero Maestro; the remains repatriated in 1869, today in the crypt beneath the Plaza de la Ciudadanía, Santiago
